A cluster whose nodes sit in two places — some on a cloud, one at home — and
whose pod traffic between them is encrypted on the wire with WireGuard. This
page builds one on OpenStack (verified on OVH Public Cloud) and proves the
encryption rather than asserting it.

The two "sites" here are both OVH instances, labelled into two *locations*,
`ovh` and `home`, so the shape can be demonstrated without a real second site.
Nothing about the method depends on that: replace the `home` node with a
machine anywhere that can reach the others over UDP, and the same configuration
holds.

## The shape

| | |
|---|---|
| One controller | `role: controller`, location `ovh`. Runs no workloads |
| One worker | `role: worker`, location `ovh` |
| One worker | `role: worker`, location `home` |
| CNI | Calico, with node-to-node WireGuard encryption |
| Datastore | Embedded etcd, on the single controller |

One controller, not three, and it is deliberate: with a single control-plane
node there is no etcd quorum to split across the WAN. If you grow this to an HA
control plane, keep all three controllers in **one** location — a quorum with
two members on one side of a link and one on the other loses itself the moment
the link does. See [the HA control plane](/docs/install/ha-cluster/).

## Why Calico WireGuard, and not Kilo

Two tools can encrypt inter-node traffic here, and the choice is worth stating.

[Kilo](https://kilo.squat.ai/) is the obvious fit for the *narrative* — it
models locations directly and can encrypt only cross-location traffic. But in
that "location" granularity it elects one gateway per location and relays
cross-site traffic through it, which is a hub per site. Kilo's `full` mesh
granularity is genuinely node-to-node, but then it encrypts everything and the
locations become cosmetic — the same outcome as Calico, reached through a
`custom` CNI and hand-applied manifests.

Calico's own WireGuard support is a **direct node-to-node full mesh with no
hub**, and it is the cleaner fit for Corium: `network.cni: calico` is a
modelled field, and the one switch that turns encryption on,
`spec.network.calico.wireguard`, is reached verbatim through `k0s.patch`. No
custom CNI, no add-on, no host WireGuard to manage — the kernel module ships in
the Fedora base, and Calico's Felix builds and keys the `wireguard.cali`
interface itself.

So: Calico WireGuard. Every node-to-node workload path is encrypted, which
includes the cross-site path; the locations remain as node labels, used for
placement and for reading `kubectl get nodes`.

## Before you start

- An OpenStack project and the `openstack` client.
- The signed Corium qcow2 for your version — see [downloads](/docs/install/downloads/).
- A flavor with 4 GB or more and a disk at least the image's 10 GiB.
- A network that gives each instance an address the others can reach. On OVH,
  `Ext-Net` hands out a public address directly, which is what the nodes use as
  their WireGuard endpoints.

## 1. Register the image (UEFI)

Corium boots UEFI only. Verify the download before trusting it — the chain is
`cosign` (who built it) then `sha256sum` (did you get those bytes); both are in
[downloads](/docs/install/downloads/). Then register it with the firmware property set:

```bash
openstack image create corium-0.3.6 \
  --file corium-0.3.6-x86_64.qcow2 --disk-format qcow2 --container-format bare \
  --property hw_firmware_type=uefi \
  --property hw_machine_type=q35 \
  --property hw_disk_bus=virtio \
  --property os_type=linux
```

`hw_firmware_type=uefi` is not optional; without it the instance boots a BIOS
firmware and never finds a bootloader. On a slow uplink, do the download,
verification and upload from a throwaway instance in the same region rather
than from your laptop — the bytes are the same and the bandwidth is not.

## 2. Key and firewall

The security group has to allow, on top of your own SSH and API access, the
traffic the nodes exchange **between themselves**. The two that are easy to
forget are the encryption ports:

| Port | Protocol | For |
|---|---|---|
| 51820 | UDP | WireGuard — the encrypted tunnel itself |
| 4789 | UDP | Calico VXLAN |
| 6443 | TCP | Kubernetes API |
| 9443 | TCP | k0s join API |
| 8132 / 8133 | TCP | konnectivity |
| 10250 | TCP | kubelet |
| 2379 / 2380 | TCP | etcd (between controllers) |

The simplest correct rule set opens SSH, ICMP and the API to you, and then lets
members talk to each other by pointing a rule at the security group itself:

```bash
openstack keypair create --public-key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub corium-wg
openstack security group create corium-wg

# external: your access
openstack security group rule create --proto tcp --dst-port 22   --remote-ip 0.0.0.0/0 corium-wg
openstack security group rule create --proto tcp --dst-port 6443 --remote-ip 0.0.0.0/0 corium-wg
openstack security group rule create --proto icmp                --remote-ip 0.0.0.0/0 corium-wg

# internal: any member to any member, covering every port in the table above
openstack security group rule create --proto tcp  --remote-group corium-wg corium-wg
openstack security group rule create --proto udp  --remote-group corium-wg corium-wg
openstack security group rule create --proto icmp --remote-group corium-wg corium-wg
```

`--remote-group corium-wg` is the load-bearing part: it says "from any instance
in this group", so WireGuard's UDP/51820 between the nodes is allowed without
enumerating addresses that do not exist yet.

## 3. The controller

[`examples/stretched-controller-calico-wireguard.yaml`](https://github.com/Corium-OS/Corium/blob/main/docs/examples/stretched-controller-calico-wireguard.yaml)
is the full document. The parts that matter:

```yaml
corium:
  role: controller
  cluster:
    name: stretched
  network:
    cni: calico
  storage:
    type: etcd
  node:
    name: corium-wg-ctl
    labels:
      corium.dev/location: ovh
  k0s:
    patch:
      spec:
        network:
          calico:
            mode: vxlan
            wireguard: true      # <- turns on the encryption
            mtu: 1350            # <- must leave room for the WireGuard header
```

Boot it, and wait for k0s:

```bash
openstack server create corium-wg-ctl \
  --image corium-0.3.6 --flavor c3-4 \
  --key-name corium-wg --security-group corium-wg --network Ext-Net \
  --user-data stretched-controller-calico-wireguard.yaml --wait

ssh core@<controller-ip> sudo k0s status      # wait for "Role: controller"
```

A `role: controller` node runs no kubelet, so it does **not** appear in
`kubectl get nodes`, and Calico's pods stay `Pending` until a worker joins —
there is nowhere for them to schedule yet. Both are expected, not a failure.

You can confirm the switch reached the rendered config before any worker exists:

```console
$ ssh core@<controller-ip> sudo grep -A3 'calico:' /etc/k0s/k0s.yaml
        calico:
            mode: vxlan
            mtu: 1350
            wireguard: true
```

## 4. The workers

The CNI is a cluster-wide decision the controller has already made, so a worker
needs only its role, a name, a location label and a join token. Mint the token
on the controller:

```bash
ssh core@<controller-ip> sudo k0s token create --role=worker --expiry=2h
```

Now write one document per worker:

1. Copy [`examples/stretched-worker.yaml`](https://github.com/Corium-OS/Corium/blob/main/docs/examples/stretched-worker.yaml) to
   `stretched-worker-ovh.yaml` and `stretched-worker-home.yaml`.
2. In each, set `join.token` to the token you just minted. Inline is fine for a
   lab; prefer `join.tokenFrom` with an HTTPS secret source otherwise.
3. Set the location label per node — `ovh` in one file, `home` in the other.

> **Warning.** The token is a live credential for the duration of its expiry.
> Treat these two files as secrets and do not commit them.

Then create both workers:

```bash
for loc in ovh home; do
  openstack server create corium-wg-w-$loc \
    --image corium-0.3.6 --flavor c3-4 \
    --key-name corium-wg --security-group corium-wg --network Ext-Net \
    --user-data stretched-worker-$loc.yaml --wait
done
```

They come up `NotReady`, then `Ready` once the Calico DaemonSet lands on them:

```console
$ ssh core@<controller-ip> sudo k0s kubectl get nodes -o wide -L corium.dev/location
NAME               STATUS   ROLES    VERSION       INTERNAL-IP     LOCATION
corium-wg-w-home   Ready    <none>   v1.36.4+k0s   57.130.75.118   home
corium-wg-w-ovh    Ready    <none>   v1.36.4+k0s   57.130.75.146   ovh
```

Each worker registers its own public address as its internal IP, which is the
address the others reach it at — and, once WireGuard is up, the endpoint of its
tunnel.

## 5. Confirm the encryption is on

Calico enables WireGuard per node and publishes each node's public key on its
`Node` object. If the annotation is there, Felix has keyed the tunnel:

```console
$ ssh core@<controller-ip> sudo k0s kubectl get nodes \
    -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" "}{.metadata.annotations.projectcalico\.org/WireguardPublicKey}{"\n"}{end}'
corium-wg-w-home  AVR4Qm9WDk1WASU+7TOTW/0rMQM78a4y20LP7EChTWc=
corium-wg-w-ovh   pR14xMuDCmEgr79raxLE12oMYVcZzwd2JKxDxMMVHX4=
```

The interface itself exists on each node, at the MTU you set:

```console
$ ssh core@<worker-ip> sudo ip -d link show type wireguard
4: wireguard.cali: <POINTOPOINT,NOARP,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1350 ...
    wireguard ...
```

### Work from your own machine

The commands from here on run `kubectl` locally rather than over SSH. Fetch a
kubeconfig once:

```bash
ssh core@<controller-ip> sudo k0s kubeconfig admin > stretched.kubeconfig
export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/stretched.kubeconfig
kubectl get nodes
```

The address in that file is the one k0s chose. Check the `server:` field points
somewhere you can reach before relying on it.

The Corium image is minimal and ships no `wg` binary. To read the live tunnel
state — handshakes and byte counters — without modifying the read-only OS, run
`wg` from a pod that shares the host's network namespace and holds `NET_ADMIN`:

```bash
kubectl run wgtool --image=nicolaka/netshoot --overrides='
{"spec":{"hostNetwork":true,"nodeSelector":{"corium.dev/location":"home"},
"containers":[{"name":"wgtool","image":"nicolaka/netshoot","command":["sleep","3600"],
"securityContext":{"privileged":true,"capabilities":{"add":["NET_ADMIN"]}}}]}}'
kubectl exec wgtool -- sh -c 'apk add -q wireguard-tools; wg show'
```

## 6. Prove it, end to end

Put two pods on two different locations and make them talk. Save this as
`proof.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: web, labels: {app: web}}
spec:
  nodeSelector: {corium.dev/location: ovh}
  containers: [{name: nginx, image: nginx:1.27-alpine}]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: client}
spec:
  nodeSelector: {corium.dev/location: home}
  containers: [{name: net, image: nicolaka/netshoot, command: ["sleep","36000"]}]
```

Apply it and wait for both to be running:

```bash
kubectl apply -f proof.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/web pod/client --timeout=120s
```

**Connectivity** — the client on `home` reaches the web pod on `ovh`. Take the
web pod's address from the cluster rather than typing one in:

```bash
WEB_IP=$(kubectl get pod web -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}')
```

```console
$ kubectl exec client -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "http://$WEB_IP"
200
$ kubectl exec client -- ping -c3 "$WEB_IP"
3 packets transmitted, 3 received, 0% packet loss
```

**The tunnel carried it** — `wg show` on the `home` node names the `ovh` node's
own address as the peer endpoint (a direct tunnel, not a relay), with a recent
handshake and non-zero counters:

```console
interface: wireguard.cali
  public key: AVR4Qm9WDk1WASU+7TOTW/0rMQM78a4y20LP7EChTWc=
  listening port: 51820
peer: pR14xMuDCmEgr79raxLE12oMYVcZzwd2JKxDxMMVHX4=
  endpoint: 57.130.75.146:51820
  allowed ips: 10.244.120.0/26
  latest handshake: 12 seconds ago
  transfer: 31.24 MiB received, 15.62 MiB sent
```

**Nothing is in the clear** — capture the underlay NIC while the pods talk.
Only WireGuard UDP/51820 crosses between the two nodes; a filter for the pods'
own HTTP (TCP/80) between them catches nothing:

```console
$ kubectl exec wgtool -- tcpdump -nni enp3s0 -c4 'udp port 51820 and host 57.130.75.146'
IP 57.130.75.118.51820 > 57.130.75.146.51820: UDP, length 176
IP 57.130.75.146.51820 > 57.130.75.118.51820: UDP, length 704
...

$ kubectl exec wgtool -- timeout 8 tcpdump -nni enp3s0 'tcp port 80 and host 57.130.75.146'
0 packets captured
```

One honest note: WireGuard here encrypts **workload** traffic — pod-to-pod and
pod-to-node. Some node-to-node Kubernetes control traffic (the kubelet API on
TCP/10250) still crosses the underlay outside the tunnel, but it is TLS on its
own account, not in the clear.

## Pitfalls

**MTU.** This is the one that bites. The 1500 B underlay carries Calico's VXLAN
(50 B) and WireGuard (60 B) headers, so the pod-facing MTU must come down to at
most 1390. This build sets `spec.network.calico.mtu: 1350` for margin. Leave it
at the default and large packets black-hole while pings and small requests
work — a failure that looks like anything but MTU.

**Control-plane placement.** Keep the etcd quorum on one side of the WAN. With a
single controller that is automatic; with three, put all three in one location.
Splitting a three-member quorum two-and-one means the minority side is dead and
the majority side is one failure from dead.

**WireGuard ingress.** UDP/51820 between nodes is what the whole thing rides on,
and a security group that only opened TCP will leave every node keyed, every
annotation present, and no handshake ever completing. Open UDP/51820 (and
Calico's UDP/4789) between members — the `--remote-group` rule in step 2 does.

## When you are done

```bash
for n in corium-wg-ctl corium-wg-w-ovh corium-wg-w-home; do
  openstack server delete "$n" --wait
done
openstack image delete corium-0.3.6
openstack security group delete corium-wg
openstack keypair delete corium-wg
```
